sum: The Cigna Group reported stronger third-quarter operations on Thursday, November 5, 2026, and raised its full-year adjusted earnings outlook. AD HOC NEWS reported that management increased the minimum 2026 adjusted income-from-operations outlook by 0.15 US dollars per share to 30.60 US dollars.

Third-quarter revenue rose 6 percent year over year to 73.7 billion US dollars. Adjusted income from operations reached 2.1 billion US dollars, or 7.98 US dollars per share, compared with 7.83 US dollars a year earlier. Reported shareholders' net income fell because the prior-year period included an after-tax gain from a business sale.

Cigna Healthcare was the main operating growth driver. Adjusted revenue increased 9 percent to 11.7 billion US dollars, while adjusted pretax income rose 15 percent to 1.2 billion US dollars. Evernorth Health Services increased adjusted revenue 6 percent to 63.8 billion US dollars, but adjusted pretax income declined 4 percent to 1.8 billion US dollars.

Pharmacy Benefit Services earnings fell 22 percent to 765 million US dollars amid large client contract renewals and strategic investments. Specialty and Care Services partly offset the decline with 15 percent earnings growth to 1.1 billion US dollars. The higher earnings floor supports the near-term outlook, but medical-cost trends and pharmacy-benefit execution remain central to valuation. The Cigna Group stock gains focus as 2026 earnings outlook rises
sum: The Cigna Group reported stronger third-quarter operating performance on Thursday, November 5, 2026, and raised its full-year adjusted earnings outlook. The Financial Times company announcement said revenue increased 6 percent from the prior-year quarter to 73.7 billion dollars for the three months ended September 30.

Adjusted income from operations was 2.1 billion dollars, or 7.98 dollars per share, compared with 2.1 billion dollars and 7.83 dollars per share a year earlier. Reported shareholders' net income fell to 1.4 billion dollars, or 5.47 dollars per share, from 1.9 billion dollars and 6.98 dollars. The company attributed the decline primarily to the absence of an after-tax gain on a sale that benefited the third quarter of 2025.

Cigna Healthcare was the stronger operating contributor. Adjusted revenue in the segment rose 9 percent to 11.7 billion dollars, while pretax adjusted income from operations increased 15 percent to 1.2 billion dollars. The company linked the improvement primarily to higher net investment income and better operating efficiency.

The segment's medical care ratio was 85.0 percent, compared with 84.8 percent a year earlier. For the full year, management narrowed its expected range to 84.2 percent plus or minus 25 basis points, while raising the segment's pretax adjusted earnings floor by 50 million dollars to 4.6 billion dollars.

Evernorth Health Services generated adjusted revenue of 63.8 billion dollars, up 6 percent from the prior-year quarter. Pretax adjusted income from operations declined 4 percent to 1.8 billion dollars. Within the segment, Specialty and Care Services earnings increased 15 percent to 1.1 billion dollars, while Pharmacy Benefit Services earnings declined amid client contract renewals and strategic investments.

The Cigna Group now expects consolidated adjusted income from operations of at least 30.60 dollars per share for 2026, an increase of 0.15 dollars from its prior projection. The outlook includes anticipated dividends and future share repurchases. Evernorth's full-year pretax adjusted earnings target remains at least 6.9 billion dollars.

Four new U.S. preventive-care panel members kept drug company stocks under federal ethics waivers
sum: Four of the eight people Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. named to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force in September own stock in drug and health companies affected by the panel's decisions, according to ethics waivers obtained by The New York Times. The waivers allowed them to serve without selling those holdings.
All four own shares of Eli Lilly and Johnson & Johnson. The holdings also include Merck, Pfizer, Novo Nordisk, CVS Health and the insurer Cigna, Newser reported, summarizing the Times findings.

The task force's grades decide which screenings, counseling services and preventive medicines most private insurers must cover without cost-sharing. That gives families a direct stake in whether its members are free of financial pressures when they review colonoscopies, depression screening or HIV prevention drugs.

The four are Dr. Patrick K. Hunter, a pediatrician; Dr. Ronald P. Karlsberg and Dr. Venkatesh L. Murthy, both cardiovascular specialists; and Dr. Dennis W. Wulfeck, a diagnostic radiologist, according to the Times.

Beyond Lilly and J&J, Hunter holds Bristol Myers Squibb and nine other companies whose work could intersect with the panel's. Karlsberg owns stock or another financial interest in Merck and 16 others. Murthy owns stock in Merck, Pfizer, Cigna and 16 others, and Wulfeck in Novo Nordisk, Pfizer, CVS Health and 17 others.

Dr. Roger D. Klein, an official at the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, estimated health holdings at no more than 15% of Karlsberg's portfolio, 20% of Murthy's and Wulfeck's, and 45% of Hunter's, the Times reported. The other four new appointees, and seven of the eight members already serving, did not receive waivers for medical industry investments.

The waivers do not say whether the shares are held directly or through a managed fund, such as a mutual fund. That distinction matters, because a person who owns a broad fund has less direct control over, and often less exposure to, any single company. The waivers say each member must consider recusing from topics with particular relevance to their holdings.

The company has nevertheless beaten Wall Street's earnings estimates in each of the four preceding quarters, raising the importance of the November release for the near-term investment case.

For full-year 2026, analysts cited by the preview expect earnings per share of 30.50 U.S. dollars, compared with 29.84 U.S. dollars in 2025. Their projection rises to 33.46 U.S. dollars for 2027. The contrast between softer quarterly earnings and higher annual estimates leaves medical-cost trends, customer retention and the profitability of contracts as central issues for investors.

The Cigna Group serves more than 185 million customer relationships across more than 30 markets and jurisdictions, according to the same analysis. The initial focus is oncology and cardiometabolic care, with rollout planned from early 2027.

The initiative is intended to reduce inefficient healthcare spending by 10 percent by 2030, according to the cited analysis. What Happened With UnitedHealth Stock This Week?
sum: Shares of UnitedHealth Group (UNH) rose 4.5% over the two trading days through Wednesday, October 14, while the S&P 500 fell 1.1%. The company reported fiscal Q3 2026 results before the market opened on Tuesday. The stock slipped 0.2% that day before posting its gain on Wednesday. Management also raised its forecast for full-year 2026 earnings. So what did the report change for someone who owns the shares?
Fiscal Q3 2026 earnings per share came in at $4.69, clearing the $4.18 analysts expected. Revenue matched estimates almost exactly at $113 billion. The surprise was in profit, not sales.
On Tuesday, the market treated the report as little news. The S&P 500 was nearly flat. UnitedHealth moved alongside CVS Health and Cigna, which also edged lower, while Elevance Health rose.

Through fiscal Q2 2026, UnitedHealth’s operating margin, the share of revenue left after the costs of running the business, returned above its level a year earlier. The margin was 4.6% in fiscal Q2 2025. It fell to 3.8% in fiscal Q3 2025 and 0.3% in fiscal Q4 2025. This margin decline occurred during a year of growing sales. In FY2025, UnitedHealthcare, the largest segment, grew revenue 15.7%, and Optum Rx grew 16.1%.

The margin then recovered to 8.0% in fiscal Q1 2026 and 7.1% in fiscal Q2 2026. Fiscal Q2 2026 revenue grew only 0.4%, so the extra profit came from keeping more of each dollar rather than selling more. On a twelve-month view, profit has not come back. Diluted earnings per share were $15.54 in the twelve months to June 2026, down from $23.08 a year earlier.

Management now expects more from 2026 than it did three months ago. On October 13, the company raised its full-year 2026 forecast for GAAP diluted earnings per share to at least $19.50, up from $18.70 in July. A forecast is not a result.
Management credited the quarter to discipline and execution across every part of the business.

sum: The Cigna Group (NYSE:CI) brings together its Cigna Healthcare insurance business and Evernorth Health Services, which covers pharmacy benefit management and specialty pharmacy operations. By diversifying its business in this way, Cigna can generate earnings from several sources. As a result, we added the company to our best blue-chip dividend stocks list.

However, the company still faces challenges such as regulatory scrutiny, pricing pressure, and rising healthcare costs. In the second quarter of 2026, Cigna's revenue grew 7% from the previous year, reaching $71.7 billion. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) climbed to $7.78, up from $7.20, and net income came in at $1.66 billion. Management expressed their confidence in continued growth by raising the 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to at least $30.45.Even with stronger earnings, some risks remain. For example, Cigna Healthcare's medical care ratio increased to 84.5% from 83.2% a year earlier, which means medical costs took up a larger portion of premiums.
Evernorth is also dealing with regulatory pressure on pharmacy benefit management and could see its margins squeezed as the industry changes how it handles rebates and drug pricing.

The Cigna Group (NYSE:CI) trades at a forward P/E ratio of 8.26, compared to a trailing P/E of 11.41. This difference shows that the market expects Cigna's earnings to rise. With a forward P/E of 8.26, the implied earnings yield is around 12.1%, compared with the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield of 5.21% on October 13, 2026. This represents a spread of approximately 6.9 percentage points, although equity earnings are uncertain and do not represent guaranteed cash returns. Of course, equity earnings aren't guaranteed cash returns, so this kind of comparison is more illustrative than direct.

Cigna's valuation has narrowed over time. According to Yahoo's data, its forward P/E was 11.26 in June 2025 and dropped to 8.87 by September 2025. Right now, Cigna's forward P/E is lower than CVS Health's 10.67, which suggests that Cigna is trading at a relative discount. However, it's important to keep in mind that the two companies differ in their business mix and risk profiles, which can affect direct comparisons.

When every day feels uncertain: How Cigna Healthcare nurse case managers support NICU families
sum: At Cigna Healthcare, care management is about meeting people where they are, especially when life doesn’t go according to plan.
- Nearly 1 in 10 U.S. babies spends time in a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU).
- NICU stays can range from a few days to several months, depending on a baby’s medical needs.
- Nurse case managers help families navigate care decisions, benefits questions, specialist referrals, and discharge planning.
- Emotional support and consistent guidance can help reduce stress during a highly uncertain time.
- Care coordination continues beyond the hospital stay as families prepare to transition home.

An increasing number of industry analysts and company disclosures are indicating costs are under control for the likes of CVS Health, Centene, Cigna, Elevance Health, Humana, UnitedHealth Group and others.

Take a report last week from Morningstar senior analyst Julie Utterback, who predicted these managed care organizations "may rebound and boost profit growth well above norms through 2030" following what she called "recent troughs."

The cost picture for health insurers should become a little more clear next month when companies start reporting their third quarter earnings. Investors and analysts who follow the companies are hoping the third quarter brings more of what companies reported in the second quarter.

UnitedHealth Group, parent of the nation's largest health insurer in UnitedHealthcare, reported more than $5 billion in second quarter net income. That came during a period this year when UnitedHealthcare's medical care ratio continued to fall.

"The second quarter 2026 medical care ratio was 86.7% compared to 89.4% in the second quarter 2025," the company said of the ratio, which is the percentage of premium revenue that goes toward medical costs. "The year-over-year decrease was driven by benefit design and pricing discipline, member mix and medical cost management initiatives."

Diversified healthcare companies like UnitedHealth, CVS Health, Cigna, Elevance Health and Humana are also hearing good news in more controversial areas of their businesses like pharmacy benefit management. Such PBMs have faced new federal and state rules and regulations and it wasn't long ago that analysts on Wall Street were speculating the vertical integration strategy of these healthcare giants would go away.

5 HMO Stocks in Focus Amid an Aging U.S. Population, Tech Innovation
sum: The U.S. health insurance industry, commonly referred to as the Health Maintenance Organization (HMO), benefits from a set of diversified, cost-effective plans that generate steady premium income and secure contract renewals. However, regulatory changes could tighten Medicaid eligibility and reduce ACA enrollment, affecting membership and reimbursements. Demand for Medicare products should remain strong as the U.S. population ages, supporting enrollment and premium growth. Investments in telehealth, AI, cloud computing and data analytics are improving efficiency, patient engagement and long-term revenue prospects despite increasing near-term costs. HMOs are also pursuing strategic mergers and acquisitions (M&A) to expand market presence and diversify operations. Industry leaders such as UnitedHealth Group Incorporated UNH, The Cigna Group CI, Humana Inc. HUM, Centene Corporation CNC and Molina Healthcare, Inc. MOH are well-positioned to capitalize on these favorable growth dynamics.

Diversified Offerings Support Enrolment Stability: Health insurers continue to strengthen their membership base by offering diversified, cost-effective plans with enhanced benefits. These offerings support steady enrollment growth, generate consistent premium income and often lead to contract wins and renewals from federal and state agencies. However, gains from diversified products are expected to only partly offset the expected Medicaid membership declines resulting from growing regulatory challenges following the enactment of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The legislation introduced stricter Medicaid eligibility checks, work requirements and reduced federal funding. These measures, coupled with the absence of ACA subsidy extensions, are likely to reduce enrollment and pressure margins, prompting insurers to focus more on higher-margin commercial plans, while anticipated Medicare Advantage reimbursement rate increases in 2026 may provide some support.

An Aging U.S. Population: Medicare plans are specifically designed to meet the healthcare needs of individuals aged 65 and older, and an aging U.S. population is expected to drive sustained demand for these products.

UnitedHealth Group UNH, the largest Medicare insurer by membership, saw a 20.7% drop in share price between Monday and Tuesday afternoon, while shares for Humana HUM plummeted 22% and CVS Health CVS fell 13.3%.

Recent trends in commercial health insurance market concentration
sum: This chart collection examines trends in market competition among commercial health insurers in the large group, small group, and individual markets using enrollment data for fully insured and individual plans using 2013-2023 data from Mark Farrah Associates. This analysis also incorporates 2013-2023 enrollment data for self-funded plans from Mark Farrah Associates for certain charts. This analysis uses three metrics of market competition: the market share of the largest insurer in each state; the number of insurers in each state with at least 5% market share; and the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI), a standard measure of market concentration across all industries.

The impact of consolidation on prices and enrollee experience depends on a variety of factors, including regulation and the market power of other healthcare stakeholders. In the context of health insurance markets, high concentration may give insurers more leverage to negotiate lower payments to providers. Conversely, a lack of competition could give insurers less incentive to lower costs for enrollees and afford purchasers less choice when seeking coverage.

While commercial health insurer participation can vary significantly within states, this analysis focuses on state-level data and national averages of market concentration data across states. This data is illustrative of trends in health insurance market competitiveness, though it may not reflect the actual geographic markets where health insurance is offered. For example, group market plans may be purchased for employees living across the country while individual market plans are typically offered at the county or local level (though in many cases insurance carriers do operate statewide).

On average, commercial health insurance markets remained highly concentrated across market segments between 2013 and 2023. However, particularly since 2020, the individual market has grown more competitive while fully insured group markets have become less competitive. More than 9 in 10 people who purchase individual market coverage do so through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplaces, and much of the coverage purchased off-Marketplace is also ACA compliant coverage and therefore mirrors plans sold on the Marketplace.

items.t: Aetna, Cigna, United called out for price transparency failures
sum: A new study published in the American Journal of Managed Care found that Aetna, Cigna and UnitedHealthcare continue to lag with healthcare price transparency compliance despite years to update their negotiated rates for the public.

The study conducted by Simple Healthcare evaluated whether the three major U.S. payers reported complete data under the Transparency in Coverage (TiC) rule, which was implemented in 2022 to enable employers and individuals to access pricing.

The TiC rule requires all commercial payers to publicly disclose in-network negotiated rates, out-of-network allowed amounts and prescription drug rates. Payers must also report the prices in a machine-readable format for all providers, updated monthly.
Failure to disclose all required rates could result in enforcement actions, including fines. However, no payer has yet been publicly fined or penalized for noncompliance.

But that doesn't mean payers are fully complying with the extensive price transparency requirements, according to the study. It found that the completeness of pricing data varied significantly across the payers.

For example, Aetna reported, on average, prices for just about half of hospital outpatient codes (51%) and 70% of hospital inpatient codes. For commonly billed codes, Aetna reported an average of 73% of cardiology billing codes, 70% of family practice codes and 86% of orthopedic surgery codes.

Meanwhile, Cigna averaged 20% of common hospital outpatient codes, 81% of hospital inpatient codes, 90% of orthopedic surgery codes and 89% of the most common cardiology and family practice billing codes.

sum: Stocks jumped Monday as a to end the federal government shutdown gained traction in the Senate, though it lacked any clear resolution to that Democrats have been fighting for.

Investor optimism for an end to the longest federal government shutdown in U.S. history buoyed the S&P 500 by 77 points, or 1.2%, to 6,806 in early Monday trading. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 320 points, or 0.7%, to 47,308, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite surged 1.8%.
Health insurers were among the losers early Monday as a lack of clarity on health care subsidies clouded their futures. Cigna shares dipped 1.7%, while Humana slipped 2%.

Sunday's test vote marked the beginning of a series of procedural maneuvers aimed at passing a compromise bill to fund the federal government, although final passage could be several days away. The Senate may hold a vote by mid-December on extending expiring health care tax credits, the key sticking point.
Monday's gains were led by a rebound in technology shares as investors' alarm over the run-up in stock prices related to the craze for artificial intelligence appeared to calm.

"Progress on a deal to end the government shutdown looks like it could give the market an early-week boost," said Chris Larkin, managing director of trading and investing at E*TRADE from Morgan Stanley, in an email.

He added, "But with a relatively light earnings calendar and continued economic data delays, sustaining any bounce may hinge on whether the market's AI leaders regain momentum after last week's setback."
